metadata.title: Labour Market Mismatch and Labour Productivity (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses micro-data from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to construct industry-level mismatch indicators, which are then linked to industry-level labour productivity measures from firm-level data. For the PIAAC component, the paper describes that PIAAC uses a matrix-sampling design and complex sampling across countries; to compute consistent sampling variance, it uses a replication technique (Jackknife Repeated Replication) and applies weights via the “PIAAC Tool” macro. For the mismatch-to-productivity regressions, the paper does not report using PIAAC student-level weights directly in the econometric model; instead, it aggregates mismatch to 1-digit industries and then estimates industry-level OLS regressions with country and industry fixed effects. The econometric specifications weight observations by the number of firms (industry size) to address outliers from small cell sizes, and standard errors are clustered at the country level.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The econometric analysis uses an overlapping set of 19 PIAAC countries for which industry-level productivity data are available, and aggregates PIAAC mismatch indicators to 1-digit ISIC market sector industries. The final dataset is restricted to 11 1-digit industries (manufacturing; utilities; construction; wholesale/retail; transport/storage; accommodation/food; information/communication; real estate; professional/scientific/technical; administrative/support). Before aggregation, the paper applies mismatch benchmark thresholds to PIAAC proficiency scores (5th/95th percentiles for the overall skill mismatch indicator; 10th/90th percentiles for industry-level links), restricts to employees with one job and excludes self-employed workers, drops ISCO codes 0 and 6, and merges ISCO codes 1 and 2. The productivity dataset further excludes firms with one employee and firms in the top and bottom 1% of the labour productivity distribution, and the regression observations are weighted by the number of firms in each country-industry cell.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper links mismatch indicators constructed from OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) micro-data to industry-level labour productivity measures derived from firm-level ORBIS data. Mismatch is defined using qualification benchmarks (ISCED vs job-required qualifications) and skill mismatch using PIAAC proficiency scores with percentile-based thresholds; the paper aggregates mismatch to 1-digit industries and estimates country-industry fixed-effects regressions for 19 OECD countries. The productivity decomposition follows Olley–Pakes (within-firm productivity and allocative efficiency), and the baseline results show that higher qualification mismatch and skill mismatch are associated with lower labour productivity, with over-skilling and under-qualification accounting for most of the effects. The study reports economically significant magnitudes (e.g., a 1 SD increase in over-skilling corresponds to ~6% lower allocative efficiency) and robustness checks including market competition and managerial quality. The analysis is explicitly correlational rather than causal, and the econometric sample is limited by availability of productivity data, so counterfactual gains for countries outside the econometric sample are more speculative.
